The callout is REPLACED with a SYMPTOM→CAUSE→FIX framing: (1) keyword anchors: 'running total wrong on tied dates, same-date rows show same running total, running total not accumulating one at a time, default frame RANGE lumps peers, ROWS vs RANGE running total, why are my cumulative values all the same on the same day, two events same day same cumulative value, running total stuck at end-of-day value'; (2) SYMPTOM verbatim: 'a running total where rows sharing the same ORDER BY value (e.g. the same date) ALL show the SAME total (the end-of-that-date cumulative), instead of accumulating one at a time'; (3) CAUSE: 'with ORDER BY date and NO explicit frame, the DEFAULT frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE includes ALL PEER rows tied on the ORDER BY value — so all same-date rows share one frame, and therefore share one cumulative value (the sum through the end of the peer group)'; (4) FIX (BOTH required): explicit `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` AND unique tiebreaker in ORDER BY (`ORDER BY day, event_id`); SQL template included; (5) ANTI-FIX DO-NOT-RECOMMEND: 'do NOT fix this symptom by relying on the default frame or switching to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — the default RANGE frame IS THE CAUSE of the symptom. Recommending it gives the user MORE of the bug they reported. If a question reads same-date rows all show the same cumulative value, how do I make them accumulate one at a time? the answer is NEVER just use the default frame / switch to RANGE / omit the frame clause — that is the bug. The answer is ALWAYS the explicit-ROWS + unique-tiebreaker pair.' Also includes 'when default RANGE IS what you want' disambiguator (peer semantics intent — Pattern 1 of the iter544 canonical is correct in that case only). WebSearch-verified at trino.io/docs/467/sql/select.html: 'If the frame is not specified, it defaults to RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, which is the same as RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW' and 'contains all rows from the start of the partition up to the last peer of the current row' — quoted in the callout.
